To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter
Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of
Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and
look forward to your mark-up.
SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)
Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims
is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.
Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and
only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the
basket is recoverable.
Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after
Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims
unless expressly stated otherwise.
Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same
caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.
Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and
non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.
Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public
registers (see Disclosure Letter).
Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the
Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or
public records.
Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller
will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the
counterparty's written consent.
Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding)

bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds

matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including

[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly
searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific
disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent,
payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2.
As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security

Buyer has completed its own verification.

must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Draft and Disclosure Letter

## Scope and caveats

- I have only the Seller's summary positions and Disclosure Letter, not the full SPA draft or the underlying data room documents (DD-002 to DD-012). Clause references are as the Seller presents them and may not match the actual draft.
- Statutory points (Limitation Act 1969 (NSW), Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), ACL and Corporations Act misleading-conduct rules, payroll tax and superannuation) are flagged for verification by NSW counsel and tax advisers before we rely on them.
- The Seller's package is a negotiating position, not a neutral summary. Its disclosure letter is drafted to shift diligence risk to the Buyer.

## Part A: Risk allocation in the Seller's SPA positions

**1. General liability cap (cl 12.1): AUD 4.8m (20% of price)**
- This caps general warranty exposure at one-fifth of the price. Given the known issues below, the cap is too low for the risks we have identified.
- *Push back:* Set a general cap at a materially higher level (e.g. 30–50% of price) and carve out fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities from it entirely.

**2. Thresholds (cl 12.2): AUD 25k de minimis, AUD 250k basket, excess-only recovery**
- The basket is a deductible: once claims pass AUD 250k, only the excess is recoverable. Combined with a AUD 25k de minimis, many individually small claims fall outside the warranty regime altogether, and the Buyer absorbs the first AUD 250k of losses.
- *Push back:* Reduce the de minimis (e.g. AUD 10k) and aggregate related claims arising from the same facts. Convert the basket to a tipping basket, so once it is exceeded the Buyer recovers from the first dollar. Exclude fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities from both thresholds.

**3. Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13): 18 months for general claims; limitation applies to all claims**
- Eighteen months is short for a business with a 30% Bluefen revenue dependency, an unresolved IP title issue and a privacy incident still under investigation. Issues often surface after one audit or tax cycle.
- The Seller's proposal that any limitation applies to all claims unless expressly stated would silently shorten the periods for fundamental and tax claims.
- *Push back:* General warranties at 24–36 months. Fundamental and title warranties at the statutory maximum (confirm the NSW position, including whether the SPA is executed as a deed). Tax claims to run until 60 days after the relevant ATO assessment period closes (confirm the period with tax advisers). Specific indemnities for the identified matters to survive until resolved. Reverse the default so that limitation applies only where expressly stated.

**4. Fundamental and title warranties subject to general caps and time limits**
- This is the most significant structural point. Capacity and title warranties go to the Buyer's ability to own what it is paying for. Subjecting them to a 20% cap and 18-month window is commercially unacceptable.
- *Push back:* Reject outright. Fundamental warranties (capacity, title to shares, authority, no encumbrances) should be capped at the full purchase price, outside the thresholds, and survive for the statutory maximum.

**5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to all claims (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)**
- The Seller proposes these apply to "Claims of any nature". That would purport to cover fraud and possibly statutory misleading-conduct claims.
- Australian law generally does not permit contracting out of ACL and Corporations Act misleading-conduct protections, and a non-reliance clause will not protect a party from its own fraud. Overbroad drafting invites dispute and may be unenforceable in part, but the Buyer should not rely on that.
- *Push back:* Carve out fraud, wilful concealment and statutory liability. Limit the non-reliance clause to Buyer's reliance on extra-contractual statements, and confirm it does not cut back the warranties themselves.

**6. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7; DL 1.1 and 1.2)**
- This is the most dangerous provision in the package. Disclosing "every fact contained or referred to" in the data room (including DD-002 to DD-012) would disclose the Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, bonus, privacy and supplier issues against every warranty. Combined with cl 8.3, it would leave the Buyer with almost no warranty recovery.
- *Push back:* Reject general disclosure. Disclosure should be specific, fair and reasonably particularised against a specific warranty. Public registers should be disclosed only to the extent of a specific search result. Data room documents should not be disclosed generically. Ask for the disclosure to be deleted in full and replaced with a specific schedule that the Buyer approves.

**7. Buyer knowledge (cl 8.3): anti-sandbagging**
- The Buyer would lose any claim for matters known to it or its advisers, including anything "discoverable from the data room or public records". This targets exactly the matters we have identified, and would reward the Seller for disclosing issues in a data room rather than in the disclosure letter.
- The position on sandbagging is not uniformly settled in Australia, so an express clause matters.
- *Push back:* Delete cl 8.3 and insert an express pro-sandbagging clause: the Buyer's knowledge does not prejudice any claim, and warranties are given as to facts irrespective of what the Buyer knows. Specific indemnities for known matters should be expressly agreed as protection for known issues.

**8. Tax and IP positions "settled under the general regime"**
- Known tax and IP exposures should not be treated as settled under the general cap and time regime. Tax liabilities of the company for pre-Completion periods should be covered by a separate tax indemnity.
- *Push back:* Standalone tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax and on-costs, uncapped to purchase price, surviving to the statutory limit. Separate IP warranties (ownership, chain of title, no infringement) with fundamental treatment for title, plus the specific Ironquay indemnity below.

## Part B: Specific diligence issues

**9. Bluefen change-control consent (DL 2; cl 3 / 6.3)**
- Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m, roughly 30% of FY26 revenue. Consent is not obtained, and the conditions in clause 11.3 are not evidenced as satisfied.
- The Seller's wording is weak: "reasonable endeavours" and treating consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent, which may not be the full consent or cover the clause 11.3 conditions.
- *Push back:* Make an unconditional written Bluefen consent, in a form acceptable to the Buyer, with all clause 11.3 conditions satisfied, a condition precedent to Completion. The Seller should procure it, not merely use reasonable endeavours. Add a long-stop date with a Buyer termination right, and a specific indemnity for loss of Bluefen revenue or termination if consent is conditional or later withdrawn.

**10. Riverlark facility (DL 3; cl 2 / 7)**
- The facility has about AUD 3.2m outstanding and is not repaid. The Seller proposes a release "following Completion". That is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal: the Buyer would acquire the company with a secured debt, and the release would depend on the bank's cooperation after the Buyer has paid.
- *Push back:* Payout letter and discharge of all security (including any share charge or PPSR registration) delivered at Completion. Repayment funded from the purchase price at Completion. Run a PPSR search against the company and the shares.

**11. Ironquay IP (DL 4; cl 11.1)**
- The IP ownership of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on payment of every SOW3 fee. AUD 180k is recorded as open, and there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment in the data room. The Seller's indemnity covers only the SOW3 payment itself, which does not protect against an IP title claim.
- Calling this "adequate" is wrong.
- *Push back:* Seller to pay all outstanding Ironquay amounts before Completion (or treat them as debt in the price mechanics), and deliver a confirmatory assignment of all SOW3 Project Materials as a condition. Require bank evidence of payment. Add a specific, uncapped indemnity for any Ironquay IP title or infringement claim, plus a warranty that no other Ironquay SOW is unpaid.

**12. Employee bonuses (DL 5; funds flow)**
- AUD 420k of Completion bonuses are conditional on Completion and continued employment, but are not in the draft funds flow, and the Seller says they are "a matter for the Seller" without itemising them.
- Bonuses of this kind are generally debt-like and will also attract employer on-costs. Superannuation at 12% on AUD 420k would be roughly AUD 50k if the payments are ordinary time earnings. Payroll tax exposure is also unquantified (verify NSW position).
- *Push back:* Treat all bonuses and employer on-costs as debt-like items and deduct them from the price, or have the Seller pay them as a pre-Completion cost. Require a schedule of all employee entitlements, with an indemnity for any undisclosed entitlements and for payroll tax and super on the bonuses.

**13. Export/privacy incident (DL 6; cl 4.6 / Schedule 6)**
- This is the most significant unquantified risk. A download link for about 1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) went to an unintended external address. The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material", which is not a basis for the Buyer to accept the risk.
- Under the Privacy Act's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, if there is an eligible data breach, the company would need to assess and potentially notify the OAIC and affected individuals. The assessment timeframe is short, so this needs urgent attention (verify with privacy counsel).
- *Push back:* Independent forensic investigation before signing, with the findings delivered to the Buyer. Specific indemnity, uncapped or separately capped at a material level, covering notification costs, regulatory action, remediation and third-party claims. Warranty that no unauthorised access has occurred except as disclosed. Consider a price holdback or escrow pending the investigation outcome.

**14. Office lease (DL 7)**
- The lease has a notification obligation, and the Seller does not confirm whether the share sale requires landlord consent.
- *Push back:* Lease review confirming whether change of control is a trigger. If so, landlord consent or waiver as a condition, or a specific indemnity for any landlord action.

**15. Supplier renewals (DL 8; "ordinary course")**
- Three Sandbar renewals total AUD 330k (three AUD 110k contracts). The disclosure says it cannot tell whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course. The Seller's characterisation is not supported by its own disclosure.
- The three equal amounts should be checked for contract splitting or threshold avoidance. That may be innocent, but it should be asked.
- *Push back:* Full copies of the contracts, termination rights and renewal terms. Any renewal relating to the pre-Completion period, or with termination costs, should be treated as a debt-like item or the subject of a specific indemnity. Confirm whether the Buyer's consent is needed for renewal.

**16. Mossvale assignment restriction (DL 9)**
- The disclosure does not say whether Mossvale's consent is required by a share sale.
- *Push back:* Legal confirmation that no consent is triggered, or obtain consent as a condition. Specific indemnity if a consent is later found to be required.

**17. Title to the shares (DL 10; DD-012)**
- The share register shows Harbourglass as holder of 100%. The Buyer has not verified this.
- *Push back:* Current ASIC company extract, certified copy of the share register and certificates, confirmation of no options, convertible instruments or other rights over shares, and a PPSR and encumbrance search. Fundamental title warranty as described above.

**18. Funds flow and price mechanics**
- The Seller says the funds flow "reflects the agreed price mechanics", but the debt-like items are not reflected in it.
- Illustration only, assuming AUD 24.0m headline price and before cash, working capital and any tax adjustments:
  - Less Riverlark: approx. AUD 3.2m
  - Less bonuses: approx. AUD 0.42m (plus on-costs)
  - Less Ironquay SOW3 open fees: approx. AUD 0.18m
  - Less Sandbar renewals if pre-Completion: up to AUD 0.33m
  - Indicative equity value: roughly AUD 19.9m–20.2m before further adjustments
- *Push back:* A full completion accounts or locked-box mechanism with a defined debt and debt-like items schedule, a funds flow reconciled to that schedule, and a specific mechanism for each item above.

**19. Document integrity**
- Clause references are inconsistent across the Seller's summary (for example, Riverlark appears under both cl 2 and cl 7, and conditions under both cl 3 and cl 6.3). The summary cannot be relied upon for drafting purposes.
- *Push back:* A consolidated mark-up of the full SPA and a clean disclosure letter reconciled to it.

## Part C: Summary recommendations

**Priority 1: Structural protections (reject the Seller's positions)**
1. Reject the application of the general cap, thresholds and 18-month limit to fundamental and title warranties. Cap at full price, survive to the statutory maximum.
2. Reject general data room and public register disclosure (Schedule 7; DL 1.1, 1.2).
3. Delete the anti-sandbagging clause (cl 8.3) and insert an express pro-sandbagging clause.
4. Carve out fraud and statutory liability from the limitation, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions.
5. Increase the general cap (30–50%), replace the excess-only basket with a tipping basket, and lower the de minimis.
6. Separate tax indemnity, uncapped to price, and separate IP warranties.

**Priority 2: Conditions and deal-breakers**
7. Bluefen: unconditional written consent as a condition precedent, with a long-stop date.
8. Riverlark: payout and discharge of all security at Completion, funded from the price.
9. Forensic investigation of the privacy incident before signing, plus a specific indemnity.
10. Ironquay: payment of SOW3 fees and a confirmatory IP assignment as conditions, with an uncapped IP indemnity.

**Priority 3: Price and specific indemnities**
11. Treat bonuses (with on-costs), Ironquay fees and any pre-Completion supplier renewals as debt-like items, with a reconciled funds flow.
12. Specific indemnities for the lease, Mossvale, supplier renewals and any undisclosed employee entitlements.
13. Title verification: ASIC extract, share register, PPSR and encumbrance searches.

**Immediate next steps**
- Ask the Seller for the full SPA draft, the underlying DD-002 to DD-012 documents, the Bluefen clause 11.3 conditions, the SOW3 payment records, and the Sandbar contracts.
- Engage privacy counsel on the DD-006 notification assessment and forensic scope.
- Engage NSW counsel to confirm the statutory points flagged above before the mark-up goes out.

**Priority 1: Structural protections (reject the Seller's positions)**
1. Reject the application of the general cap, thresholds and 18-month limit to fundamental and title warranties. Cap at full price, survive to the statutory maximum.
